article.overview: A hydrogen detector is an instrument designed to find and map hydrogen in lunar material. The main interest is that hydrogen concentrated in cold, permanently shadowed polar regolith could indicate water ice. Hydrogen is not usually measured directly from orbit. Most lunar hydrogen detectors instead count neutrons produced when cosmic rays strike the surface, because hydrogen-rich material slows these neutrons and changes the neutron signal that escapes. Two flown examples are the Lunar Prospector Neutron Spectrometer (1998–1999) and the Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND) on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). A 2025 proposed compact epithermal neutron counter is included as a non-flown example.
article.description:
A hydrogen detector is a scientific instrument that measures how much hydrogen is present in the surface material of a planetary body, usually by mapping the neutrons that the surface emits. The Moon is bombarded continuously by galactic cosmic rays. When these high-energy particles strike the regolith, they release neutrons. Some of these neutrons escape to space, and their energy distribution carries information about the material they passed through. Hydrogen nuclei have almost the same mass as neutrons, so collisions with hydrogen remove a large share of a neutron's energy. Regions rich in hydrogen therefore produce fewer escaping neutrons at the energies that detectors are designed to count.

The catalogue entry "Hydrogen detector" is a general measurement goal rather than one standard design. The catalogue also lists a separate entry for neutron-based hydrogen detectors (No. 101). The two categories overlap in practice, and this article covers entry 100 through the examples below, all of which are neutron-based.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The primary purpose of a lunar hydrogen detector is to determine where hydrogen is concentrated and in what form it may be present. The LRO LEND instrument was specified to produce hydrogen distribution maps with a sensitivity of 100 ppm hydrogen and a spatial resolution of 5 km, and to characterise the surface distribution and column density of possible near-surface water-ice deposits [1]. The same instrument package was also intended to build a global model of thermal-energy neutron radiation at 30–50 km altitude [1].

Applications include locating candidate water-ice deposits in permanently shadowed craters, guiding the choice of sites for future missions, and providing context for impact and volatile-transport studies. Because the Moon's poles are a potential water resource for crewed and robotic exploration, the mapping has a practical as well as a scientific purpose.
article.operating_principle:
The instruments described here do not look for hydrogen with a chemical analyser. They count neutrons and sort them by energy. Neutrons are commonly grouped into thermal (very slow, below about 0.25 eV), epithermal (intermediate energy) and fast (high energy) ranges. Epithermal neutrons are particularly useful for hydrogen mapping because they are strongly moderated by hydrogen. Thermal neutrons are also affected by hydrogen and by other elements that absorb neutrons.

Neutrons are counted by gas proportional counters filled with helium-3. When a neutron is captured by a helium-3 nucleus, the reaction produces charged particles that deposit energy in the gas and create an electrical pulse. Energy discrimination is achieved with shielding. Cadmium absorbs thermal neutrons, so a cadmium-covered counter responds only to higher-energy neutrons. The Lunar Prospector Neutron Spectrometer used this approach: one counter had a 0.75 mm cadmium shield and was sensitive only to epithermal neutrons above 0.25 eV, while the other had a 0.75 mm tin shield and was sensitive to thermal and epithermal neutrons [2]. The difference between the two counts gives the thermal neutron flux [2]. The hydrogen abundance is then inferred by comparing observed neutron counts with models of the neutron environment. The hydrogen is not identified directly by the neutron counts alone.
article.scientific_importance: The polar hydrogen question is important because permanently shadowed craters may preserve volatile material over long periods. Water ice there would be a resource for future exploration and a record of volatile delivery to the Moon. The 1998 Lunar Prospector result drew attention to the poles [7]; LEND later produced higher-resolution hydrogen maps [1]; and the LCROSS impact in 2009 reported water in the Cabeus plume [4][8]. Interpreting hydrogen as water is not automatic, however. Hydrogen can also be delivered by the solar wind and retained in cold regolith, and the 2010 Science papers on LEND and LCROSS are the primary references for how these interpretations were resolved [5].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a hydrogen detector. The values below describe three specific instruments: two flown neutron spectrometers and one proposed compact counter. They are not comparable in a strict sense, because the flown instruments were built as part of large spacecraft missions and the proposed counter is a conceptual design. Values are reported only where a checked source states them.

examples.name: Lunar Prospector Neutron Spectrometer (NS)
examples.detector_configuration: Two identical helium-3 gas proportional counters, each 5 cm in diameter and 20 cm long. One counter has a 0.75 mm cadmium shield (sensitive only to epithermal neutrons above 0.25 eV); the other has a 0.75 mm tin shield (sensitive to thermal and epithermal neutrons).
examples.mounting: One of the three Lunar Prospector booms, on a chassis shared with the Alpha Particle Spectrometer.
examples.overall_dimensions: Not stated in the PDS catalogue entry; only per-counter dimensions are given.
examples.operation: Designed to operate continuously during the primary mission.
examples.primary_goal: Search for water ice in permanently shadowed areas near the lunar poles.
examples.qualification: Flight instrument; mass and power as stated in the PDS catalogue entry.

examples.name: Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.detector_configuration: Four high-pressure helium-3 proportional counters, each with a cadmium foil cover, inside the collimator module; four further helium-3 detectors outside the collimator (one epithermal sensor and three thermal sensors). Configuration reported in a calibration and validation study; not verified against the primary instrument paper in this run.
examples.mounting: Mounted directly on the spacecraft body because the collimator's relatively high mass is reported to have prevented a boom deployment.
examples.qualification: Mass and power were not stated in the PDS instrument description and were not found in the sources checked. Values are null, not estimated.

examples.name: Proposed compact epithermal neutron counter (2025)
examples.type: Proposed conceptual design; no laboratory prototype, engineering model, test campaign or flight reported
examples.dimensions: Present configuration fits within a standard 1U envelope (no physical dimensions in mm given; simulated silicon sensor is 1 cm × 1 cm × 750 μm).

power_consumption_w.status: Conflicting values in the source; both are recorded.

examples.sensor: Boron-coated (10B) fully depleted silicon imager detecting alpha and 7Li reaction products; benchmark sensor is a Teledyne CIS-120 back-illuminated scientific CMOS; 3 μm 10B layer.
examples.claimed_sensitivity: Sensitivity to H2O weight fractions as low as 0.01 wt% for a 10 cm² active area. The exposure time is given as 15 minutes in the abstract and 5 minutes in the body; the figure is from Monte Carlo simulation.
examples.claimed_efficiency: 5–10% for 0.4 eV–500 keV neutrons (body section 4.2.2); 7% in the conclusion.
examples.test_status: No environmental, thermal or qualification testing reported. Simulations run in a vacuum environment. Deployment on CubeRover-class platforms is proposed, not confirmed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The three examples differ widely in scale and status. The Lunar Prospector NS consists of two 5 cm × 20 cm helium-3 counters inside a spacecraft-mounted instrument whose overall dimensions are not stated [2]. LEND dimensions were not found in the sources checked [1][6]. The proposed counter is said to fit within a standard 1U envelope [3]. A new hydrogen detector would need its dimensions set by the required sensitivity, shielding and collimation, and by its mounting.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: For spacecraft engineering, mass is normally expressed in kilograms. The NS has a stated mass of 3.9 kg [2]. LEND mass was not found [1]. The proposed counter has a simulated mass of 154 g before margin, or 231 g with a 50% margin as stated in the paper [3]. Mass determines launch and integration requirements, so the difference between a small proposed counter and a flown boom-mounted spectrometer is significant for mission design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Lunar Prospector NS uses about 2.5 W [2]. The LEND power was not found [1]. The proposed counter's power is given as about 1.64 W in the text and about 1.5 W in the table, a conflict in the source that remains unresolved [3].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A hydrogen detector in lunar orbit operates in a vacuum with strong temperature variation between sunlight and shadow, and under continuous cosmic-ray bombardment. The instrument must maintain stable detector temperatures and resist radiation effects. Its counts are sensitive to background neutrons produced by the spacecraft itself and by the instrument's own materials, so background must be separated from the lunar signal. A calibration study of LEND notes that this separation is a central analysis challenge [6]. Pointing and collimation matter for spatial resolution. A surface-deployed unit would also need stable ground contact and protection from thermal and mechanical disturbance. These are general engineering considerations and are not drawn from a verified specification for any single instrument.
article.limitations: Neutron counts give only an indirect measure of hydrogen. The result depends on models of the neutron environment, surface composition and instrument background. The depth from which neutrons escape is limited, so the instrument samples the upper part of the regolith rather than the full thickness of any ice deposit. Spatial resolution is limited by the collimation and orbital geometry; LEND's stated resolution is 5 km [1]. Hydrogen maps cannot by themselves distinguish water ice from other hydrogen-bearing material.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The flown examples are orbital payloads, so the relevant sequence is spacecraft integration, launch, cruise, orbit insertion, commissioning, and then operation with pointing, thermal and data interfaces. The proposed compact counter is discussed for future small rover-class platforms, but no interface with any named rover, lander or spacecraft has been verified [3].
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into the spacecraft (orbiter) on Earth, with mounting on a boom for the Lunar Prospector NS and direct body mounting for LEND [2][6].
Launch on the spacecraft's launch vehicle; Lunar Prospector launched in January 1998 on an Athena II [7].
Cruise to the Moon and insert into lunar orbit.
Commission the instrument and bring its detectors to operating temperature.
Operate the instrument with the spacecraft's pointing, thermal and data systems.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The flown instruments were not surface-deployed. The Lunar Prospector NS was mounted on a boom [2]. LEND was mounted directly on the spacecraft body because its collimator's mass prevented a boom deployment [6]. A proposed surface counter would need a deployment method appropriate to its platform; none is specified in the source [3].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Lunar Prospector NS (1998–1999) and the LEND instrument on LRO are flown orbital examples [2][1][7]. The proposed 2025 compact counter is a non-flown example [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility assessment with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is made. A surface hydrogen detector's compatibility would need its mass, dimensions, mounting, landing loads, power, deployment method and communications interfaces checked against verified specifications. The proposed counter's rover-class deployment is a concept only [3].

article.historical_significance:
The Lunar Prospector Neutron Spectrometer measured a hydrogen-related signal near both poles in 1998, and this was interpreted as water in permanently shadowed craters [2][7]. The interpretation is not unique: a competing explanation attributes the polar neutron depression to hydrogen implanted by the solar wind and retained in the cold polar regolith. The LEND instrument on LRO later mapped hydrogen at higher resolution and produced the sensitivity and resolution figures used in this article [1][5].

The LCROSS mission impacted Cabeus crater on 9 October 2009. News coverage of the mission reported that water had been found, and that LRO's neutron sensor had earlier that year indicated strong hydrogen [4]. Coverage of the 2010 Science papers reported that water ice made up about 5.6% of the mass in the plume, with an uncertainty of ±2.9%, and that the LEND hydrogen signal was not mostly attributable to water [8]. These statements come from secondary coverage and should be checked against the primary papers before use.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name "hydrogen detector" describes a measurement goal rather than one standard design. The flown examples measure neutrons, not hydrogen directly, so hydrogen abundance is an inference that depends on models of the neutron environment, the surface composition and the instrument background. Values such as mass, power and sensitivity must be tied to a named instrument and source. The proposed Tiffenberg counter has simulated but untested performance, with an unresolved power figure and exposure-time inconsistency [3]. LEND mass and power were not found in the sources checked [1]. The primary 1998 Lunar Prospector papers and the primary 2010 Science papers were not opened in this run; some statements rely on secondary sources. Image assets were not verified for this article, so no figures are included.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image objects are included because no direct image asset URL could be verified in this run; image arrays are intentionally empty rather than containing unverified or null-URL entries.

data_quality_notes: Image assets: no direct image asset URL was verified from an official page in this run, so the master registry and all section arrays are empty. No image URLs were invented.
LEND mass and power: not stated in the PDS instrument description and not found in the other sources checked. Values are null.

Proposed counter (Tiffenberg 2025): power is given as about 1.64 W in the text and about 1.5 W in the table; exposure time for the 0.01 wt% sensitivity is 15 minutes in the abstract and 5 minutes in the body. Both conflicts are reported as found. The 154 g unmargined mass total is a sum of the table entries, and the 231 g margined total is as stated in the paper.

Secondary-source claims: the LEND detector configuration and the statement that the collimator mass prevented a boom deployment come from a search summary of arXiv:2104.03451, whose full text was not accessible (HTTP 404 on the PDF URL). The LCROSS 5.6% ±2.9% water-ice figure and the statement that the LEND hydrogen signal was not mostly water come from secondary coverage of the 2010 Science papers.

Primary papers not opened: the 1998 Lunar Prospector hydrogen papers and the 2010 Mitrofanov et al. Science LEND paper (science.org returned HTTP 403; the DOI record could not be verified). The Mitrofanov author list, volume and pages are unverified and are marked as such in the references.

Unverified background figures: the Lunar Prospector NS polar sensitivity (about 100 ppmw) and the later LEND polar-regolith average (about 105 ppmw above 80° latitude, about 140 ppmw above 88°) appeared only in search summaries and are not stated in this article.

Lunar Prospector launch and impact: the January 1998 launch on an Athena II and the 31 July 1999 impact date come from secondary sources and search summaries, not from a primary NASA page opened in this run.

Competing interpretation of polar epithermal neutron depression (water ice vs solar-wind hydrogen): this is stated from a literature summary without a primary citation; it should be checked against the primary 1998 paper.
Duplicate-topic note: catalogue entry 101 (Neutron-based hydrogen detector) overlaps with entry 100. This article describes entry 100 only and does not reuse facts from any other payload article.
